Putrid

/PYOO-trid/ - the stress falls on PYOO · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Putrid means rotting and giving off the smell of decay.

One putrid potato at the bottom of the sack announced itself through the closed pantry door.

Worked Example

Dairy farmers fear a torn silage tarp more than a hailstorm: let air reach the pit and the winter feed goes putrid in a stripe a yard deep — black, sweetish, and useless. Old hands walk the tarp weekly and weight every gap with split tires, because one small leak can cost a season's hay.

Putrid is the exact word for that ruined stripe, because it means rotting and giving off the smell of decay — the smell is written into the definition. Rotten tells you the state; putrid adds the announcement, the reek of decomposition that reaches you well ahead of the sight. Flesh, feed, and vase water go putrid. Dust and old paper never do; they only go musty.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rotten: the everyday word for decayed; putrid adds the overpowering smell of advanced decay

decayed: broken down by time and microbes, smell optional

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sweet: clean to the nose

unspoiled: not yet touched by decay

Where it sits · how close the smell is to rot — musty → rank → putrid

musty vs. putrid: Musty is the mild rung — the closed-closet smell of damp and long disuse.

rank vs. putrid: Rank goes further than musty — strong enough to turn your head at a distance — but putrid claims the most: the unmistakable reek of something actually rotting.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — putr

Root — putr: rotten (Latin puter, putrere)

Suffix — -id

Suffix — -id: adjective ending: in a given state

Put it together

Put it together: Putr- (rotten) + -id (in that state) = in a rotten state. Latin putrere, "to rot," gives the pair English still uses side by side: putrefy, the process, and putrid, the arrived condition — with the smell folded into both.

Use the root in a new word: putrefy

Use the root in a new word: putrefy: Field guides warn that a catch left unbled will putrefy by evening in tropical heat.

Root Check

Word Choice

blunt / visceral

Putrid is the strongest of this unit's smell words and the most specific: real decay, actually under way — flesh, food, cut flowers in old water. Rancid is narrower still, for fats and oils gone over; fetid is standing air and water; noisome is the broad umbrella for anything offensive. If nothing is decomposing, putrid overstates.
